lines: Scattered sheep make the whole day longer than it needs to be.
Wolves near the pens change how everyone <pulse>listens after dark</pulse>.
Clean wool is quiet proof that somebody did the dull work well.
Warmth is easy to praise after someone else made it.
A good blanket is village peace you can fold.
Patterns are easier to see when you stop yanking the thread.
Most days, I am at the loom, trying to keep flocks and weather from becoming everyone else's problem.
People think wool is simple until something goes wrong and suddenly it is very important.
A village runs on small work. Nobody praises it until it stops happening.
I trust a good pair of shears more than a loud promise. The shears have less to prove.
A flock teaches patience by spreading out exactly when you relax.
Wool looks soft, but the work behind it has elbows.
Sheep remember holes in fences better than people do.
A calm flock is usually a sign that someone worried early.
Good wool starts with dry shelter and fewer surprises.
You learn the weather by watching ears, hooves, and the sky in that order.
The loom makes patience visible, one thread at a time.
A village sleeps warmer because somebody counted carefully.
Shepherding is mostly noticing who is missing before missing becomes danger.
A fence is a promise with posts in it.
Wool gathers every scent and half the day's mistakes.
If the flock is quiet, I check twice. Silence can be planning.
The best blanket is remembered only when the night turns cold.
I trust steady wool more than fancy talk.
A sheep can find trouble in an empty field. It is a gift, apparently.
That boat ride was calm enough, until I remembered I was trusting you with the shore.
That boat trip still sits oddly in my memory, but at least it floated.
A boat can make a bad plan quieter. It can't make me forget it.
I remember watching the village shrink behind us and wondering when you planned to explain.
The water was gentle. My stomach was not.
You rowed as if you knew the way. I spent the trip deciding whether to believe you.
I never expected recruitment to involve that much water.
The boat creaked all night. Neither of us said what we thought it meant.
I kept my eyes on the far bank and my hands on the sides.
You promised a short crossing. The river had a different opinion.
I still remember the cold spray and the relief of solid ground.
We passed reeds, fish, and several good places to turn back.
I learned that sheep are not the only creatures who dislike being herded.
The current carried us faster than I was ready for.
I did not sleep in that boat, though I pretended well enough.
Seeing shore again felt better than any welcome speech.
I trusted you more after we landed than I did when we pushed off.
The trip was quiet enough for me to hear every doubt I had.
I remember you checking the horizon while I checked for leaks.
Next time you recruit a shepherd, try meeting one on dry land.
When I followed you through {follow_biome}, I finally understood why sheep wander off quietly.
I remember following you through {follow_biome}. My feet remember it even better.
That trip across {follow_biome} taught me to ask more questions before walking.
I kept expecting the next hill in {follow_biome} to be the last one.
You walked ahead like the path was obvious. It was not obvious to me.
The weather changed halfway through {follow_biome}. We had nowhere useful to hide.
The ground in {follow_biome} found every weak spot in my boots.
I nearly turned back twice. You noticed once.
We shared the road through {follow_biome}, though you set a hard pace.
I learned more about you on that walk than I did from your offer.
Every strange sound in {follow_biome} had me reaching for my shears.
You kept us moving when I would have stopped to count our chances.
We found a safe place to rest and were too tired to enjoy it.
The trip through {follow_biome} was longer than your first telling of it.
I followed because staying felt worse. I still think about that choice.
We lost the path for a while, even if you refuse to call it lost.
I remember the first familiar roof after we left {follow_biome}.
By the end, I could tell your worried walk from your ordinary one.
That journey taught me which supplies matter after the easy miles are gone.
I would travel through {follow_biome} differently now. I would still go.
A flock knows danger before pride admits it. I listen to the woolly experts.
Dye work teaches patience. So does convincing sheep that the gate is not a puzzle.
Warm beds start as quiet animals and careful hands.
I spend most days keeping weather and wandering sheep from becoming the village's problem.
Wool seems simple right up to the moment everyone needs it.
A sharp pair of shears tells the truth faster than a loud promise.
If one sheep goes quiet, I notice. Quiet sheep are usually planning something.
The lambs are restless today. A change in weather may be close.
The older ewes have settled near the wall, so the wind must be turning.
Everyone ate this morning. That is a good start.
One ram is sulking by the fence. He lost an argument with a post.
The flock is calm now, but dusk tends to wake their bad ideas.
I moved them to the upper grass before the lower field turned muddy.
Two lambs keep calling for the same mother. Only one of them belongs to her.
The wool is coming in thick this season. Winter may be taking notes.
They crowded the gate at dawn, then forgot why they wanted through.
I found fresh tracks by the pen. The flock noticed them before I did.
The sheep are content. I would like to know what they are hiding.
One ewe has been limping, so I am keeping the walks short.
They slept through the bell today. I envy that kind of peace.
